meanings.short: Describes a separation, direction or path in spacetime that something slower than light could follow.
meanings.long: Two events are timelike separated when light could cross the distance between them with time to spare. A clock carried from one to the other measures the proper time between them, and every observer agrees which of the two came first.

meanings.short: Describes a separation, direction or surface in spacetime that not even light could cross in the time available.
meanings.long: No signal can link spacelike separated events, so neither can cause the other. Some observer sees them happen at the same moment, and different observers can disagree about which came first.

everyday: In everyday English null means empty or void; in relativity it means separated exactly as light travels.

meanings.short: Describes a separation or path that light could follow exactly, so the spacetime interval along it is zero.
meanings.long: Null (also called lightlike) is the borderline case between timelike and spacelike. Light rays travel on null paths, and along them no proper time passes.

meanings.short: A single point in space and time: a place together with a moment, such as a firecracker going off.
meanings.long: Events are the basic objects of relativity. An event is labelled by four numbers, three for position and one for time; observers in different frames give the same event different labels.

meanings.short: One of the possible outcomes of a random process, or a set of them, to which a probability can be given.
meanings.long: In probability an event is something that may or may not happen, such as a coin landing heads or a count in a detector within a given second.

meanings.short: A single recorded occurrence in an experiment or survey, such as one particle hitting a detector or one star brightening as a lens passes.
A single recorded occurrence in an experiment, such as one particle hitting a detector.
A single point in space and time: a place together with a moment.
Something that happened: here, a stage in the history of the universe.
Unchanged by a given transformation, such as moving to another frame, turning the axes or changing the gauge.
meanings.long: A quantity is invariant under a transformation when it keeps the same value afterwards; a law is invariant when it keeps the same form. The speed of light and the spacetime interval are invariant under Lorentz transformations, while lengths and time differences are not.

meanings.short: Of a subspace: sent into itself by an operator, so the operator turns every vector of the subspace into another vector of the same subspace.
meanings.long: A one-dimensional invariant subspace is spanned by an eigenvector. The whole space and the zero vector alone are always invariant.

meanings.short: The change in the frequency of a wave when its source and the observer move towards or away from each other.
meanings.long: An approaching source is heard or seen at a higher frequency, a receding one at a lower frequency. For light the shift in frequency is the Doppler shift; in relativity time dilation adds an extra factor, so there is a shift even for motion across the line of sight.

meanings.short: The shift in frequency of light from a source moving across the line of sight, caused purely by the slowing of its clocks.
meanings.long: Classically, motion at right angles to the line of sight gives no Doppler shift. In relativity the moving source's clock runs slow by the Lorentz factor, so its light arrives at a lower frequency even then.

meanings.short: The change in the direction from which light seems to arrive, caused by the observer's own motion.
meanings.long: Running through vertical rain, you see the drops slant towards you; light behaves similarly. As the Earth's velocity changes over a year, every star seems to move around a small ellipse, up to about 20 arcseconds either side of its mean position. In relativity aberration bunches the light from all directions towards the direction of motion.

meanings.short: The equation that gives the expansion rate of a uniform universe from its density and the curvature of space.
meanings.long: In words: the square of the Hubble rate equals 8πG/3 times the mass density, minus a curvature term k c² over the scale factor squared. Alexander Friedmann found it from general relativity in 1922; a Newtonian argument gives the same form.

meanings.short: The equation that gives how fast the expansion of a uniform universe speeds up or slows down, from its mass density and pressure.
meanings.long: In words: the second time derivative of the scale factor, divided by the scale factor, equals minus 4πG/3 times the sum of the density and three times the pressure over c². Pressure adds to gravity's pull, and a negative pressure, as of vacuum energy, makes the expansion speed up.

meanings.short: The rule used before relativity to convert positions and times between two frames in steady relative motion: clocks agree, positions shift by velocity times time.
meanings.long: For a frame moving at speed v along x, the new position is x minus v t, and time is unchanged. It works well at everyday speeds but does not keep the speed of light the same in every frame, which is why relativity replaced it by the Lorentz transformation.

meanings.short: The principle that the laws of mechanics take the same form in every frame moving at constant velocity, when frames are related by Galilean transformations.
meanings.long: Newton's laws are Galilean invariant: no mechanical experiment inside a smoothly moving ship can reveal its speed. Maxwell's equations are not, which was one of the clues that led to special relativity.

everyday: Not rising prices: in cosmology inflation means a brief burst of extremely rapid expansion of space.

meanings.short: A proposed burst of enormously fast expansion in the first tiny fraction of a second, which made the universe smooth and flat.
meanings.long: During inflation a field in a high-energy state drives the expansion to grow exponentially, doubling the size of the universe many times. It explains why the universe is so uniform and so nearly flat, and quantum ripples stretched by it became the seeds of galaxies. Alan Guth proposed it in 1980.

meanings.short: A stretch between two values or two moments; in maths, all the numbers between two end points.
meanings.long: A time interval is the time between two instants. In maths the interval from a to b contains every number between them; it is closed when the end points are included and open when they are not.

meanings.short: The spacetime interval: the one combination of the time and distance between two events that all observers in steady motion agree on.
meanings.long: In words, the squared interval is the squared distance minus c² times the squared time difference (some courses use the opposite sign). Its sign tells whether the separation is timelike, spacelike or null.

meanings.short: The one combination of the time and distance between two events that all observers in steady motion agree on.
meanings.long: In words, the squared interval is the squared distance between the events minus c² times the squared time between them (some courses use the opposite sign). Lengths and times differ between frames, but this combination does not, which makes it the natural measure of separation in spacetime.

meanings.short: The energy a body has because it is moving.
meanings.long: At everyday speeds it is half the mass times the speed squared. In relativity it is the total energy minus the rest energy, which grows without limit as the speed approaches that of light.

meanings.short: The proposal, made around 1890, that bodies moving through the aether shrink along their motion, invented to explain why Michelson and Morley saw no effect.
meanings.long: FitzGerald (1889) and Lorentz (1892) suggested that motion through the aether squeezes a body by just the factor that hides the motion. Relativity later gave the same shrinking a different meaning, as length contraction between frames, with no aether at all.

meanings.short: The shortening of a moving object along its direction of motion, as measured by an observer it moves past.
meanings.long: An object of proper length L, moving at speed v, is measured to be L divided by the Lorentz factor. Only the length along the motion changes, and the effect is noticeable only near the speed of light.

meanings.short: The distance between two distant objects measured at one moment of cosmic time, as a chain of rulers laid end to end would give it.
meanings.long: In an expanding universe the proper distance to a galaxy is the scale factor times its comoving distance. It grows as the universe expands, and its rate of growth gives Hubble's law, but it cannot be measured directly.

meanings.short: The spacetime length of a spacelike separation: the distance between two events in the frame where they happen at the same time.
meanings.long: For spacelike separated events it is the square root of the spacetime interval, the spatial counterpart of proper time.

meanings.short: The spacetime length of a spacelike separation: the distance between two events in the frame where they happen at the same time.
The distance between two places measured along space with the metric at one fixed time, as rulers laid end to end would give it.
meanings.long: In Schwarzschild spacetime the proper distance between two spheres is larger than the difference of their r coordinates, because space near the mass is curved.

meanings.short: The length of a path through spacetime, measured with the metric; for a massive particle the quantity that matters is its proper time.
A measure of speed used in relativity, chosen so that speeds along one line combine by simple addition; it grows without limit near light speed.
meanings.long: Rapidity η is defined by tanh η = v/c. At low speed it equals v/c, but as v approaches c it grows without bound. A boost by rapidity η mixes time and position the way a rotation mixes two directions, with hyperbolic functions in place of sine and cosine.

meanings.short: The principle that in any small freely falling laboratory all the laws of physics take the same form as in special relativity.
meanings.long: It extends the weak equivalence principle from falling bodies to every law of physics. It is what lets general relativity describe gravity as the curvature of spacetime.

meanings.short: The principle that gravity itself falls in a gravitational field: bodies held together by their own gravity fall like everything else.
The principle that no local experiment can tell a uniform gravitational field apart from an acceleration of the laboratory.
meanings.long: It follows from the equality of inertial and gravitational mass, so that all bodies fall alike. Experiments confirm it to about one part in 10¹³ and better.

meanings.short: The distance from one crest of a wave to the next.
meanings.long: For any wave, the speed equals the wavelength times the frequency. Visible light has wavelengths of about 400 to 700 nanometres; radio waves can be metres or kilometres long.

meanings.short: The four-component quantity combining the electric potential and the magnetic vector potential, which changes between moving frames as an event's coordinates do.
meanings.long: Its three space components are the vector potential and its time component is the electric potential. The electric and magnetic fields follow from its derivatives, and Maxwell's equations take a compact form in terms of it.

meanings.short: The four-component quantity made from charge density and current density, which changes between moving frames as an event's coordinates do.
meanings.long: Its three space components are the current density and its time component is the charge density times c. Because it transforms this way, a moving charge density appears as a current, which is how magnetism follows from electricity and relativity.

meanings.short: The 4 × 4 table of numbers that converts the time and position of an event from one inertial frame to another.
meanings.long: Multiplying an event's four coordinates by the Lorentz matrix gives its coordinates in the other frame. For a boost along x it mixes only x and ct, with entries made from the Lorentz factor and v/c, and it keeps the spacetime interval unchanged.

everyday: Not a push: a boost changes the observer's frame, not the motion of the object.

meanings.short: A change of viewpoint to a frame moving at constant velocity relative to the first, with no turning of the axes.
meanings.long: In relativity a boost along x is a Lorentz transformation that mixes x and time. In spacetime it acts like a rotation through a hyperbolic angle, the rapidity, and two boosts in the same direction add their rapidities.

meanings.short: A change of viewpoint to a frame moving at constant velocity relative to the first, with no turning of the axes.
A rejected idea that the Earth carries the supposed light-carrying aether along with it, so that our motion through the aether could not be detected.
meanings.long: Aether drag was meant to explain the null result of Michelson and Morley. It was ruled out by the aberration of starlight and by Fizeau's 1851 measurement of light in moving water.

meanings.short: A rejected idea that light leaves its source at a fixed speed relative to that source, so light from moving sources travels faster or slower.
meanings.long: Emission theories tried to keep Galilean addition of velocities for light. Observations of binary stars and of gamma rays from fast-moving particles show the speed of light does not depend on the source's motion.

meanings.short: Matter made of antiparticles, which have the same mass as ordinary particles but opposite charge; matter and antimatter destroy each other on meeting.
meanings.long: The antiparticle of the electron is the positron. Annihilation turns all the rest energy into radiation, far more energy per kilogram than any chemical or nuclear fuel; the observed universe contains almost no antimatter.

origin: Latin annihilare, to reduce to nothing (nihil).

meanings.short: The destruction of a particle and its antiparticle when they meet, turning their energy into other particles such as photons.
meanings.long: An electron and a positron, for example, annihilate into two gamma-ray photons. In the early universe annihilation removed most particles once the temperature fell too low to make new pairs.

meanings.short: Of an operator: turning a state or vector into zero. An annihilation operator, in particular, removes one quantum from a state.
Of an operator: turning a state or vector into zero. An annihilation operator, in particular, removes one quantum from a state.
Complete destruction.
The scattering of a photon by an electron, in which the photon loses energy and its wavelength becomes longer.
meanings.long: Treating the photon as a particle with energy and momentum, conservation of both gives the change in wavelength, which depends only on the scattering angle. Arthur Compton's 1923 measurement of it convinced physicists that light comes in photons.

meanings.short: The law that two electric charges attract or repel with a force proportional to each charge and to one over the square of their distance.
meanings.long: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. In SI units the force is the product of the charges divided by 4πε₀ r²; its form matches Newton's law of gravity.

meanings.short: The rule giving the force on a charge from electric and magnetic fields: charge times electric field, plus charge times velocity crossed with magnetic field.
meanings.long: The electric part pushes along the field; the magnetic part acts at right angles to both the velocity and the field, so it bends the path without changing the speed. It can be derived from the electric force and special relativity.

meanings.short: The need for a quantity to be set to a very precise value, for no known reason, so that a theory matches what we see.
meanings.long: A theory is fine-tuned when it works only if some number is chosen with great precision, as when two large contributions must cancel almost exactly. Physicists take such a coincidence as a hint that a deeper explanation may be missing.

meanings.short: The observation that some constants of nature seem to lie in a narrow range that allows stars, chemistry and life.
meanings.long: Changing certain constants, such as the dark energy density or the Higgs field's value, by a small amount would apparently make a universe without complex structure. Whether this needs an explanation, and which one, is an open question.

meanings.short: The splitting of a heavy nucleus, such as uranium, into lighter nuclei, which releases energy.
meanings.long: The pieces are more tightly bound per nucleon than the original nucleus, so their total mass is slightly smaller; the missing mass appears as energy. Nuclear power stations use fission.

origin: Latin fundere, to pour or melt.

meanings.short: The joining of light nuclei, such as hydrogen, into a heavier one, which releases energy; it powers the Sun.
meanings.long: Nuclei must collide fast enough to overcome their electric repulsion, which needs temperatures of millions of degrees. The product is more tightly bound, so its mass is slightly less than that of the parts, and the difference appears as energy.

meanings.short: Melting: the change from solid to liquid.
A brief, extremely bright flash of gamma rays from a distant galaxy, lasting from a fraction of a second to minutes.
meanings.long: Gamma-ray bursts come from billions of light years away. Because light of all energies from one arrives together, they test whether the speed of light depends on wavelength.

meanings.short: An instrument that splits light into two beams and recombines them, so tiny differences in path length shift a pattern of bright and dark bands.
meanings.long: Where the two beams meet in step they add up; out of step, they cancel. Michelson and Morley used one to compare the speed of light in two directions; LIGO uses kilometre-long ones to detect gravitational waves.

meanings.short: The puzzle of why the night sky is dark if the universe is infinite, unchanging and evenly filled with stars.
meanings.long: In such a universe every line of sight would end on a star, and the sky would be as bright as the Sun's surface. The universe's finite age, so that light from far away has not yet reached us, and the redshift of distant light resolve it.

meanings.short: The energy a body has even when at rest, equal to its mass times the speed of light squared.
meanings.long: The total energy of a moving body is the Lorentz factor times its rest energy; the extra part is kinetic energy. Rest energy can be released, as in nuclear reactions and annihilation.

meanings.short: The energy needed to pull a bound system, such as a nucleus or an atom, apart into its separate pieces.
meanings.long: A bound system has less energy, and so slightly less mass, than its parts apart. For nuclei the binding energy per nucleon is largest near iron, which is why fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy ones both release energy.

meanings.short: A narrow bright or dark line in a spectrum, at a wavelength set by a particular kind of atom or molecule.
meanings.long: Atoms emit or absorb light only at wavelengths matching the jumps between their energy levels. Bright lines come from hot thin gas, dark lines from cooler gas in front of a hotter source; their pattern identifies the element, and their shift measures motion.

meanings.short: The equations of general relativity that say how matter and energy curve spacetime.
meanings.long: In words: a measure of the curvature of spacetime, the Einstein tensor, equals 8πG/c⁴ times the stress–energy tensor, which describes the matter and energy present. Together with the rule that free bodies follow geodesics, they make up general relativity.

meanings.short: A pulsar orbiting another neutron star, whose orbit shrinks exactly as general relativity predicts from the energy carried away by gravitational waves.
meanings.long: Discovered by Hulse and Taylor in 1974 (PSR 1913+16), it gave the first evidence for gravitational waves. The pulsar's regular pulses make it a precise clock, and the measured shrinking of the orbit earned Hulse and Taylor the 1993 Nobel Prize.

meanings.short: The chain of nuclear reactions by which the Sun fuses hydrogen into helium.
meanings.long: Two protons fuse to deuterium, which captures another proton to make helium-3; two helium-3 nuclei then make helium-4 and release two protons. In all, four protons become one helium nucleus, and about 0.7% of their mass becomes energy.

meanings.short: The rule for combining velocities: how fast something moves in one frame, given its velocity in a second frame that itself moves.
meanings.long: At everyday speeds the velocities simply add. In relativity the combined speed of u and v along one line is (u + v)/(1 + uv/c²), which never exceeds the speed of light.

meanings.short: The result that the work done on a body by the total force acting on it equals the change in its kinetic energy.
meanings.long: Work is force times distance along the motion, added up over the path. The theorem holds in relativity too, with the relativistic kinetic energy.

meanings.short: Einstein's 1905 theory of space and time for observers in steady motion, built on the speed of light being the same for all of them.
meanings.long: Its consequences include time dilation, length contraction, the relativity of simultaneity and E = mc². Space and time combine into one spacetime, and the Lorentz transformation replaces the Galilean one.

meanings.short: Einstein's 1915 theory of gravity, in which mass and energy curve spacetime and freely falling bodies follow the straightest possible paths through it.
meanings.long: It rests on the equivalence principle and the Einstein field equations. It explains the bending of light, the slowing of clocks low in a gravitational field, Mercury's orbit, black holes and the expansion of the universe.

meanings.short: All the paths light can take to or from one event; it divides spacetime into that event's possible future, its possible past and the rest.
meanings.long: Drawn with time upward, light from an event spreads out on a cone. Events inside the future cone can be affected by the event, events inside the past cone can affect it, and events outside cannot be linked to it at all.

meanings.short: The path of an object through spacetime: where it is at every moment.
meanings.long: On a spacetime diagram a body at rest has a vertical world line and a moving body a tilted one. The proper time along a world line is the time a clock carried along it measures.

meanings.short: The puzzle that a twin who travels away and back returns younger than the stay-at-home twin, though each sees the other's clock run slow.
meanings.long: There is no contradiction: the travelling twin changes frame on turning round, so the two situations are not symmetric. The straight world line between two events has the longest proper time.

meanings.short: The factor by which moving clocks run slow and moving lengths shrink; it is 1 at rest and grows without limit near light speed.
meanings.long: Written γ, it equals 1/√(1 − v²/c²). It is barely above 1 at everyday speeds. A body's total energy is γ times its rest energy.

meanings.short: An unstable particle like a heavy electron, about 207 times its mass, that decays in about two millionths of a second.
meanings.long: Muons made by cosmic rays high in the atmosphere reach the ground in large numbers only because their clocks run slow at nearly the speed of light, a direct check of time dilation. Seen from the muon's own frame, the same result appears as the atmosphere being shortened by length contraction.

origin: Greek peri, near, and helios, the Sun.

meanings.short: The point of a planet's orbit closest to the Sun.
meanings.long: The opposite point is the aphelion. Mercury's perihelion slowly turns around the Sun; general relativity explains the part that Newtonian gravity and the pull of other planets cannot.

meanings.short: The hot, dense early state from which the whole observable universe has been expanding for about 13.8 billion years.
meanings.long: The Big Bang theory describes how the universe expanded and cooled from that state. Its main evidence is the expansion itself, the cosmic microwave background and the abundances of the light elements.

meanings.short: The freedom to change the potentials in certain ways without changing the electric and magnetic fields they describe.
meanings.long: Adding the gradient of any function to the vector potential, and subtracting its time derivative from the electric potential, leaves the fields unchanged. A choice that fixes this freedom, such as the Lorenz gauge, often simplifies the equations.

meanings.short: The freedom to change coordinates slightly without changing the physics, which removes four of the ten parts of a weak gravitational field.
The length of an object measured in the frame where it is at rest; every other observer measures it shorter.
meanings.long: Every other observer, moving along the object's length, measures it shorter by the Lorentz factor. All observers agree on the proper length itself, so it is invariant.

meanings.short: The length of a path through spacetime, measured with the metric.
The 1887 experiment that looked for the Earth's motion through the supposed aether by comparing the speed of light in two directions, and found none.
meanings.long: An interferometer compared light travelling along and across the Earth's motion. The expected shift of the bright and dark bands never appeared; special relativity later explained why.
